_readme: The scene manifest. One record per beat. Design fields (id, time, act, spectacle, camera, setPiece) are read by the set pieces; where a beat sits on the scroll, and for how long, is score.json; content fields (kicker, title, body, tags, staged, log and the per-beat extras under 'copy') are read by the captions. Rewriting copy never moves a scene. A beat with flagship: true is numbered F-01, F-02 … in page order, and {flagships} in an interlude kicker becomes their range, so adding a flagship never renumbers by hand. Every time is staged.

beats.title: You go home.
beats.body: In 33GOD, agents are hired, seated and reviewed. They have directors and managers, a mailroom, a clock on the wall and a records room that forgets nothing. All of it answers to one mission statement. The company has been at work the whole time. And it works for you.

copy.secondary: Watch what happens after you leave your desk.

log.subject: bloodbank.cli.session.ended
log.note: You go home. Your team is just getting started.

beats.title: Not like employees. Employees.
beats.body: Everyone hunts for the best way to work with agents. The answer is plainer. Every problem a company has with people maps one to one onto agents, so a hundred years of practice applies. Agents have memory and skills, cooperate, make mistakes and respond to incentives. With the right guidance, a small team of green agents ships enterprise work. A team of geniuses can be managed into the ground. Hold the standup. Run the kaizen.

interlude.line: Four bylaws. Everything else follows from them.

beats.title: Every agent is an employee.
beats.body: Stop orchestrating a swarm. Staff a company. A good manager does not throw up his hands and blame someone. What separates a company that grows is how it manages mistakes and what it learns. That rests on the human's moment-to-moment decisions, not the prompt or the model. There is no ceiling.

copy.quoteSource: One of the pillars that guide how 33GOD is built.

departments.name: FLUME
departments.line: The org chart, and the HR department behind it.
departments.detail: Hires directors, managers and project managers, then onboards, seats and reviews them. If the agents are the staff, Flume is the org chart.

departments.name: KREBS
departments.line: Runs every ticket's lifecycle, from filed to closed, on any board.
departments.detail: One lifecycle for every ticket, identical on every board. Whatever ticket provider sits underneath, work moves from filed to closed the same way.

departments.name: BLOODBANK
departments.line: Every memo in the building travels on one bus.
departments.detail: Every service, agent and component announces what it did and picks up its work from one bus. Every message follows a strict schema, so a new department plugs in without anyone else changing.

departments.name: CANDYSTORE
departments.line: Every event ever sent, kept and searchable.
departments.detail: Stored, indexed, embedded and searchable by meaning. The record also feeds synthesized roll-ups across many dimensions, like the daily report.

departments.name: CANDYBAR
departments.line: One clock fires every recurring job. There is no second clock.
departments.detail: Cron, rebuilt on the bus. One heartbeat ticks every minute and everything scheduled is a consumer of it. No crontab, no private timers.

departments.name: SKILLEX
departments.line: One catalog of skills, taught to every agent.
departments.detail: Skills are declared in manifests and composed by reference, then exposed to every agent CLI. A new skill reaches every employee at once.

departments.name: GENESIS
departments.line: The agent clients talk to. A contractor for hire.
departments.detail: A client talks to one Genesis agent and never sees the building. It takes the request, brings in the right departments and hands back the result.

departments.name: MILKSHAKE
departments.line: Turns usage and cost into client billing.
departments.detail: Reads vendor costs, applies the billing rules, issues the statements and reconciles against Mercury. Every cent is tracked, every change goes through a command.

departments.name: CURATOR
departments.detail: A hierarchy of small agents, each the expert on one folder. Each sees only its own territory; work that crosses branches goes up to the nearest common ancestor.

departments.name: CRANK
departments.line: Keeps work moving while you are out of the office.
departments.detail: Answers questions and makes the hard calls for you, with one goal: unblocked tickets.

departments.name: INFRA-DOCTOR
departments.line: Walks the building and puts out fires.
departments.detail: Probes the homelab every minute and repairs what it is allowed to: a stuck service restarts, a stalled stack gets recovered, and every repair is capped and cooled down. Anything bigger comes to you.

departments.name: HOLOCENE
departments.line: Where you look. Who is working, what is stuck, what needs you.
departments.detail: The operating surface: the web dashboard, Holocene Auto, the Telegram mini-app, the artifact gallery, the launch tracker and live app monitoring.

beats.title: Built from scratch, on purpose.
beats.body: Almost every part of 33GOD was written for it, to one strict set of rules: layered abstraction, one owner for every building block, extension over rewrites, reuse over copies. So each new component plugs in instead of rewiring the rest.

copy.note: Lower layers never call higher ones. Every block has one owner.

beats.title: The company runs on itself.
beats.body: For its whole life, 33GOD has run every project its builder touches, itself included. Every rough edge becomes a ticket. The ticket finds the manager who owns the fix. The fix ships back into the thing that found it. Three years of that, every day.

beats.body: Enrichment passes comb the transcript and find every project it touched. The calls are made by Jev, Typesafe's System One model, built for one job: quick, typed, yes-or-no judgments.

beats.kicker: Four people, one desk, one microphone.
beats.title: No Zoom? No problem. Speakers still get labeled.
beats.body: All diarization is backed by a custom-built voice-fingerprint service, so people are told apart by their voices, not by which laptop they dialed in from. The room is the meeting.

beats.kicker: There is no “teach it a word” button. There does not need to be.
beats.title: It learns your vocabulary. Nobody asked it to.
beats.body: Project names, people and jargon join a self-evolving dictionary as they are spoken, and Jev decides what earns a place. Nothing is configured. It works because everything is connected.

beats.body: Decisions and commitments become tickets through Pilot, a custom ticket-provider abstraction over Plane, Linear and Trello. Each ticket already knows which board it belongs to.

interlude.line: And then it starts to read like fiction.

beats.title: PJangler. The project factory.
beats.body: A project registry and bootstrapper. Every project is built from a vetted pipeline template, so on day one it already has a ticket board, a git repo, its own project manager and its own Open Notebook. A mobile app gets one more hire: a Launch Director, who works with Google and Apple to see it through a smooth launch.

beats.title: The Gateway. Every model, under one name.
beats.body: A provider-agnostic, multi-tenant LLM gateway with a multi-tiered, role-based router. Employees ask for a role, never a model, and never have to care which provider answers. The router paces every subscription against its own usage windows, reset times, burn rate and cooldowns. When a pool runs out, the chain knows where to go next: subscriptions, then metered, then free, held to 90% of each daily cap.

copy.aside: Cache tokens from every provider are counted one way, in one ledger. A thread stays with its model while its cache pays off. When it moves, its whole history goes with it.
copy.cardNote: Three roles: orchestrator, subagent, fast. Seven rungs. Every tenant gets the same roles, and each person's own subscriptions are walled off and spent first.
copy.punch: Pool 01 just ran dry. Not one window flickered.
copy.stamp: Counted from the gateway's route catalog, 20 Nov 2026: 112 routes, and a free family of 43 models in 13 pools. Tonight's dry pool and new free pool are staged.

decisions.line: 01 resets soonest, so it spends first. Nothing expires unused.
01 is out until 09:00. 02 is furthest ahead of schedule, so it takes the work. Metered starts only when every subscription is spent.
Every night at 04:37 a scout goes looking for one more free provider. When one qualifies, it signs up, tests it and deploys it.

transcript._readme: Staged words for Act III. Marked spans: {p:…} a project Jev finds, {w:…} a word the dictionary learns. 'ticket' is the index of the ticket a line becomes.

lines.text: Okay. {p:Holocene} first. The {w:stuck-work panel} still shows tickets that closed yesterday.
That's the {w:lifecycle lag}. I'll take it. Fixed by Thursday.
While we're in there, {p:HeyMa} dropped the last minute of Tuesday's call.
Then somebody decide the {p:Shortwave} pairing flow.
Decision: pair by QR, no codes. I'll write it up.
Last thing. {p:Candybar} owns the {w:nightly digest} now, not a cron.

tickets.title: Fix the lifecycle lag on the stuck-work panel
Recover the last minute of Tuesday's call
Move the nightly digest onto the clock
